What is the Bamum ruler called?
reference_answer: The king (mfon), who is also called the Sultan.

reference_answer: King Mônjù, who reigned from 1461 to 1498.

question: When did King Ibrahim Njoya reign?

question: When was King Njoya exiled by the French authorities?

reference_answer: Over 500 syllabic signs, according to AFP. Britannica counts 510 pictographic characters in the first system.

question: How did the Bamum script develop?
reference_answer: It evolved through six stages between 1897 and 1931, after a first version called Lerewa or Lewa was finished around 1897.

question: What inspired King Njoya to create a writing system?
reference_answer: A revelatory dream, according to Africa History Extra.

question: When was the Foumban Royal Palace built?

reference_answer: No. It is on Cameroon's tentative list, since 2006 according to one source.

question: When did the Museum of the Bamoun Kings open and how large is its collection?
reference_answer: It opened in Foumban in 2024 with about 12,500 pieces.

question: When did construction of the Museum of the Bamoun Kings begin?
reference_answer: In 2013, launched by King Ibrahim Mbombo Njoya because the palace rooms were too small.

question: Has the Nguon of the Bamoun people been recognised by UNESCO?
reference_answer: Yes. It is on UNESCO's List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

question: How many traditional chiefdoms is Cameroon thought to have?
reference_answer: About 13,500 across its ten regions. This is an estimate and not an official count.

question: Which decree organises traditional chieftaincies in Cameroon?
How many classes of traditional chiefdom does Cameroonian law recognise?
reference_answer: Three: first, second and third class.

question: What is the legal status of traditional chiefs in Cameroon?
reference_answer: They are recognised as auxiliaries of the administration.

question: What does a first-class chiefdom cover?
reference_answer: At least two second-class chiefdoms, and in principle no more than a division (department).

question: Who recognises a first-class chief?
What does a second-class chiefdom cover?
reference_answer: At least two third-class chiefdoms, and in principle no more than a subdivision (arrondissement).

question: Who recognises a second-class chief?
What does a third-class chiefdom cover and who recognises its chief?
reference_answer: The chief's village of origin. The Senior Divisional Officer recognises the chief by a prefectural order.

question: What monthly allowances were fixed for traditional chiefs by a 2013 presidential decree?
reference_answer: 200,000 FCFA for first class, 100,000 FCFA for second class and 50,000 FCFA for third class, according to Cameroon Tribune.

question: What titles do traditional rulers use in Cameroon?
reference_answer: Fo (Fon), Mfo, Lamido, Mey and, in some Muslim chieftaincies, Sultan, depending on the region.

question: Which regions use the title lamido for traditional rulers?
reference_answer: The Far North, North and Adamawa regions.

question: Which title do traditional rulers of the Northwest grassfields use?
What are the four cultural areas used to describe traditional dress in Cameroon?
Which peoples traditionally wore batik as ritual dress?
reference_answer: The Bamileke, Bamoun and Bamenda peoples of the west. It is now worn by all Cameroonians.

question: Where does the toghu come from?
reference_answer: Bamenda and the grassfields of the Northwest Region.

question: What is a toghu?
reference_answer: An embroidered velvet outfit, often a sleeveless vest. It was once reserved for royalty and dignitaries.

question: What is ndop?
reference_answer: A handwoven, resist-dyed cloth, often indigo blue, from the Grassfields and the Bamileke Plateau.

question: How is ndop used?
reference_answer: As a royal display cloth at ceremonies and festivals, as funerary cloth, and as a gift between elites.

question: Where are ndop patterns said to come from?
reference_answer: Cloth from eastern and central Nigeria brought by Hausa traders.

question: Which people does the kaba ngondo come from?
reference_answer: The Duala (Sawa) of the Littoral Region.

question: When is the kaba ngondo often worn?
reference_answer: During the annual Ngondo festival. It is now also a national outfit.

question: Where do the variants of the loincloth (bazin, wax, serrated) have their origins?
When is Youth Day celebrated in Cameroon and what does it commemorate?
reference_answer: On 11 February. It commemorates the 1961 unification and honours young people.

question: What does National Day, celebrated on 20 May in Cameroon, mark?
reference_answer: The replacement of the federal structure by a unitary state in 1972.

question: On what date is Labour Day in Cameroon?
Which Cameroonian public holiday is also the anniversary of independence from France?
reference_answer: New Year's Day, 1 January. Independence was on 1 January 1960.

question: On what date is Assumption Day in Cameroon?
On what date is Christmas Day in Cameroon?
Which public holidays in Cameroon have a fixed date?
reference_answer: New Year's Day (1 January), Youth Day (11 February), Labour Day (1 May), National Day (20 May), Assumption Day (15 August) and Christmas Day (25 December).

question: Where is the Ngondo festival held?
reference_answer: On the banks of the Wouri River in Douala.

question: When is the Ngondo festival held?
reference_answer: In December, often in the first week.

question: What is the highlight of the Ngondo festival?
reference_answer: A ceremony of the jengu, a water spirit in Sawa belief.

question: Has the Ngondo been recognised by UNESCO?
reference_answer: Yes. It is recognised as intangible cultural heritage, and the first anniversary of the recognition was marked in December 2025.

question: In which town is the Ngouon festival held?

question: In which languages is Muna Moto spoken?

question: What is ndolé?
reference_answer: A spicy stew of bitterleaf greens with peanut paste, meat, shrimp and pork rind. It is often described as the national dish of Cameroon.

question: What is ndolé usually served with?
Which part of Cameroon is ndolé associated with?
reference_answer: The coastal Duala (Sawa) area of the Littoral Region.

question: What is koki made from?
reference_answer: Mainly black-eyed peas and red palm oil, steamed in banana or plantain leaves.

question: What is achu soup?
reference_answer: Pounded cocoyam served with an orange or yellow soup made with red palm oil, also called yellow soup.

question: Which peoples is achu soup a staple of?
reference_answer: The Tikar and Ngemba peoples of the Northwest and West regions. It is also a traditional food of the Kom.

question: What is eru?
reference_answer: A stew of forest vine leaves (Gnetum) cooked with palm oil, crayfish, smoked fish and cow skin.

reference_answer: Poulet Directeur Général, or Director General chicken. It is chicken cooked with fried plantains and vegetables.

reference_answer: Sources disagree. Some say Douala in the 1980s and others say Yaoundé in the 1970s.

How many regions does Cameroon have?

How many subdivisions (arrondissements) does Cameroon have?
reference_answer: 360 according to Wikipedia. An older source counted 315 as of 1999, so the number has grown over time.

question: Who heads a region of Cameroon?
reference_answer: A governor appointed by the President of the Republic.

question: Who heads a department (division) of Cameroon?
reference_answer: A divisional officer called a préfet, appointed by the President of the Republic.

question: Who heads a subdivision (arrondissement) of Cameroon?
reference_answer: An assistant divisional officer called a sous-préfet.

question: What are the smallest administrative units in Cameroon?
reference_answer: Districts, run by district heads (chefs de district). They are found in large subdivisions and in regions that are hard to reach.

question: When did Cameroon's provinces officially become regions?
reference_answer: By presidential decree of 12 November 2008 (Décret N° 2008/376).

question: Which two regions of Cameroon were once part of British Cameroons?
reference_answer: The Northwest and Southwest regions. The other regions were part of French Cameroun.

question: Which three regions are the northernmost regions of Cameroon?
reference_answer: The Far North, North and Adamawa regions.

question: Which Cameroonian regions are on the coast?
reference_answer: The Littoral and Southwest regions are on the coast, and the South Region lies on the Gulf of Guinea.

question: Which four regions make up western Cameroon?
reference_answer: The Littoral, Southwest, Northwest and West regions.

question: When did the Northwest and Southwest regions receive special status?
reference_answer: In December 2019, which gave them additional powers.

question: What is the capital of Cameroon?
reference_answer: Yaoundé is the political capital. Douala is the economic capital.

question: When was the Dja Faunal Reserve inscribed as a World Heritage Site?
How did the Dja Faunal Reserve's status change over time?
reference_answer: A hunting reserve in 1950, a wildlife reserve in 1973, a Biosphere Reserve in 1981 and a World Heritage Site in 1987.

question: Who is allowed to hunt by traditional methods in the Dja Faunal Reserve?
reference_answer: The Baka. Farming and professional hunting are banned.

question: Which Cameroonian park is part of the Sangha Trinational World Heritage Site?
reference_answer: Lobéké National Park. The site is shared with Congo and the Central African Republic and was inscribed in 2012.

question: When did Cameroon get its first cultural World Heritage Site?
reference_answer: On 11 July 2025, when the Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape of the Mandara Mountains was inscribed.

question: Where is the Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape?
reference_answer: In the Far North Region, in the Mayo-Tsanaga Department, in the Mandara Mountains on the border with Nigeria.

question: What is the Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape made of?
reference_answer: Sixteen dry-stone archaeological sites in seven villages, with agricultural terraces and sites of worship, dating from the 12th to the 17th centuries.

question: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites does Cameroon have?
reference_answer: Three as of July 2025: the Dja Faunal Reserve (1987), the Sangha Trinational (2012) and the Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape (2025). Check UNESCO for later inscriptions.

question: Which Cameroonian rites are on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list?
reference_answer: The Nguon rites of the Bamoun people and the Ngondo of the Sawa.

question: When did Cameroon ratify the World Heritage Convention?
When and as what did Germany establish its colony in Cameroon?
reference_answer: On 5 July 1884 as a protectorate, which became the colony of Kamerun.

question: What were the capitals of German Kamerun?
How did German rule in Cameroon end?
reference_answer: British, French and Belgian forces invaded in 1914, and the German army surrendered in 1916.

question: How was Cameroon divided after the First World War?
reference_answer: On 28 June 1919 it was split into two League of Nations mandates, French Cameroun (the larger, eastern part) and the British Cameroons.

question: What replaced the League of Nations mandates over Cameroon in 1946?
reference_answer: United Nations trusteeships. French Cameroun became a trust territory on 13 December 1946.

question: What was the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC)?
reference_answer: A nationalist party founded around 1948 that opposed French rule and campaigned for reunification of East and West Cameroon.

question: When did French Cameroun become independent, and who was its first president?
reference_answer: On 1 January 1960, as the Republic of Cameroon. Its first president was Ahmadou Ahidjo.

question: What did the 1961 plebiscite in the British Cameroons decide?
reference_answer: The southern part chose to join the former French Cameroun, and the northern part voted to join Nigeria.

question: What happened on 1 October 1961?
reference_answer: Southern Cameroons joined the Republic of Cameroon to form the Federal Republic of Cameroon, with two federated states, East Cameroon and West Cameroon.

question: What were the capitals of the two federated states of the Federal Republic of Cameroon?
reference_answer: Yaoundé for East Cameroon and Buea for West Cameroon.

question: Who was the first president of independent Cameroon and for how long did he serve?
When did Cameroon become a unitary state and what was it called?
reference_answer: On 20 May 1972 the federal structure was replaced, and the country was renamed the United Republic of Cameroon on 2 June 1972.

question: What happened to Cameroon's provinces in 1983?
reference_answer: Centre-South was split into Centre and South, and North was split into Adamawa, North and Far North.

question: What is the nickname of the Cameroon national football team?
How many times has Cameroon won the Africa Cup of Nations?
Who did Cameroon play in its first international match?
reference_answer: Belgian Congo, in 1956. Cameroon lost 3 to 2.

question: When did Cameroon first qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations?
reference_answer: In 1970, but it went out in the first round.

question: Where did Cameroon finish when it hosted the 1972 Africa Cup of Nations?
reference_answer: Third. It lost to the eventual champions Congo.

question: How did Cameroon win its first Africa Cup of Nations in 1984?
reference_answer: It beat Nigeria 3 to 1 in the final, with goals from René N'Djeya, Théophile Abega and Ernest Ebongué.

question: Who captained Cameroon to its first Africa Cup of Nations title?
When did Cameroon first qualify for the World Cup?
What did Cameroon achieve at the 1990 World Cup?
reference_answer: It became the first African team to reach the World Cup quarter-finals, losing 3 to 2 to England in extra time.

question: Which holders did Cameroon beat in the opening match of the 1990 World Cup?
Who scored twice in extra time against Colombia at the 1990 World Cup?
When and where did Cameroon win Olympic football gold?
What record did Roger Milla set at the 1994 World Cup?
reference_answer: At 42 he became the oldest player to score at a World Cup finals, against Russia.

question: Who are some of Cameroon's most famous footballers?
reference_answer: Roger Milla, Thomas N'Kono and Samuel Eto'o are named by Wikipedia. FIFA also lists Marc-Vivien Foé and Rigobert Song as former stars.

question: Has Cameroon ever won the FIFA World Cup?
reference_answer: No. Its best result is the quarter-finals in 1990.

question: When did the Cameroon women's national team play its first game?
reference_answer: On 15 June 1991, in Nigeria. It lost 2 to 0.
